procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated February 8, 1968 of the Mysore High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 215 of 1966.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Second Class Magistrate acquitted Tara Chand of offenses under Section 135 of the Customs Act and Rule 126P(2) of the Defence of India Rules. The Superintendent of Central Excise and Customs (the complainant) appealed the acquittal under Rule 126P(2) to the Mysore High Court. The High Court disagreed with the Magistrate, convicted Tara Chand under Rule 126P(2), and sentenced him to six months of rigorous imprisonment. The acquittal under Section 135 of the Customs Act was not challenged in the High Court appeal.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Tara Chand appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's judgment and order. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's conviction under Rule 126P(2).

issue.issue_text: Whether the charge levelled against the appellant was vague or different from the one for which he was convicted.

facts: The appellant argued that the charge against him was vague and different from the one for which he was ultimately convicted.
He claimed that this vagueness caused him prejudice in his defense.

The original complaint had clearly stated all the relevant facts, detailing that the appellant was found in possession of 16 pieces of gold with foreign markings, which were concealed in pouches inside a pillow case.
application: The Court noted that the appellant never complained during the trial that the charge was vague or outside the scope of the complaint.
More importantly, the Court highlighted that the appellant, in his own statement in court, had admitted to all the relevant facts alleged by the prosecution.
The Court reasoned that because the appellant admitted to the key facts, he could not have been prejudiced in his defense, even if one were to assume the language of the charge was wide.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, finding no force in the contention. It concluded that the charge was not vague or different from the conviction, and that the facts, which were alleged, proven, and admitted by the appellant, clearly brought his case within the scope of the rule under which he was convicted.

issue.issue_text: Whether the prosecution was instituted by a person not duly authorised to do so.

facts: The appellant was initially acquitted by the trial court on the grounds that the complaint was not filed by a competently authorized officer.

The trial court reasoned that the relevant notifications authorized the Collector of Central Excise to institute a prosecution himself, but not to delegate that power or consent to someone else instituting it.
The High Court disagreed, convicted the appellant, and held that the Collector was lawfully empowered to authorize the Superintendent of Central Excise to prosecute the appellant.
The Collector of Central Excise had issued a document (Ex. P/5) which accorded his sanction to the prosecution of the appellant.
law: Rule 126Q of the Defence of India Rules states that a prosecution for the relevant offence can only be instituted "by, or with the consent of," the designated authority.
Government notifications specified that an officer not inferior in rank to the Assistant Collector of Central Excise was the designated authority for this purpose.
application: The Supreme Court focused on the plain language of Rule 126Q, specifically the phrase "by, or with the consent of."

The Court interpreted this to mean that the designated authority (like the Collector) had two options: either institute the prosecution personally or give consent for the prosecution to be instituted by another person.
The Court found that the Collector, in document Ex. P/5, had lawfully exercised the second option by according his sanction or consent.

The Court also added a practical consideration, noting the "multifarious activities" of high-ranking officers. It reasoned that the law's purpose is served when a responsible officer applies their mind to the decision to prosecute, while the subsequent procedural steps, like filing the complaint, can be lawfully carried out by others.
To interpret the rule otherwise, the Court stated, would be an unduly strict reading that would thwart the real purpose of the law.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, concluding that the prosecution was validly instituted. The Collector was fully authorized by the rules and notifications to give his consent for the prosecution to be initiated by another officer, and he had done so.

issue.issue_text: Whether the amended Gold (Control) Act, 1965, which does not prescribe a minimum sentence, should be applied instead of the law in force at the time of the offense.

facts: The appellant committed the offense on November 16, 1963.
At the time of the offense, the governing law was Rule 126P(2)(ii) of the Defence of India Amendment Rules, 1963.
This rule prescribed a mandatory minimum sentence of six months imprisonment.
Subsequently, the Gold (Control) Act, 1965 was passed, which repealed the old rules and did not prescribe a minimum sentence.
The appellant argued that this new, more lenient law should be applied to his sentencing.
law: The general legal principle is that a case is governed by the law that was in force at the time the offense was committed.
application: The Court noted that the appellant's counsel could not point to any provision of law, principle, or precedent that would justify applying the new 1965 Act to an offense committed in 1963.
The Court explicitly stated that the case must be governed by the law as it existed at the time of the offense.
Because the offense occurred in 1963, the rules from that year, including the provision for a minimum sentence, were the applicable law.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that the law in force at the time the offense was committed in 1963 must be applied. Therefore, the minimum sentence of six months imprisonment under Rule 126-P(2)(ii) was mandatory, despite the subsequent change in the law.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A case must be governed by the law in force at the time of the offense, and therefore, any minimum sentence prescribed by that law must be applied, even if the law is subsequently amended to remove such a minimum sentence.
obiter: The argument that notifications delegating the authority to prosecute must be construed strictly is not persuasive.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found that the prosecution was validly instituted, as the government notifications, when read as a whole, properly empowered the Collector to authorize the Superintendent of Central Excise to prosecute the appellant. Furthermore, the conviction was proper because the admitted facts of the case clearly fell within the scope of the rule under which the appellant was charged. Finally, the sentence was upheld on the principle that the case must be governed by the law in force at the time the offense was committed, which included a mandatory minimum sentence, irrespective of any subsequent amendments to that law.
legal_tests_applied: A criminal case must be governed by the law in force at the time the offense was committed.
Government notifications conferring authority should be read as a whole to determine their scope and intent, rather than being construed so strictly as to defeat their purpose.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that the charge was vague failed because the facts alleged and proved, which the appellant had admitted, clearly brought the case within the mischief of the rule he was convicted under.

The appellant's submission that the government notifications must be construed strictly to only allow the Assistant Collector to prosecute personally, and not to authorize another, was not accepted by the court.

The appellant's contention that the amended Gold (Control) Act, 1965, which prescribed no minimum sentence, should apply was rejected because the court held that the case must be governed by the law as it was in force at the time of the offense.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position on the validity of the charge was upheld because the court found that the facts alleged and proved clearly brought the appellant's case within the mischief of rule 126H(2)(d).

The respondent's argument that the prosecution was duly authorized succeeded because the court, agreeing with the High Court, concluded that the government notifications lawfully empowered the Collector to authorise the Superintendent of Central Excise to prosecute the appellant.

The respondent's position on sentencing was affirmed because the court applied the legal principle that the law in force at the time of the offense governs the case, which in this instance included a minimum sentence of six months under rule 126-P(2)(ii).
